Mech Tactical Wargame (6mm / 1:285)

Sci-fi Tactical Wargame · 1:285 ratio · top of machine

This mech tactical game runs at a small 6mm epic scale, which flips the usual advice upside down. The war machines are chunky enough that FDM handles them well, but they are small enough that judging detail at this size takes practice. Getting a war machine onto or off the arguably-irrelevant base is where most sizing conversations start.

FDM print settings

6mm war machines are small but chunky, so a 0.2mm nozzle with fine layers keeps the profile clean. Print several at once on one plate for efficiency and prefer upright orientations to reduce supports.

At 6mm, my advice is to think about the war machine's silhouette rather than fine texture. The analog scale matters, but what reads on the table is the overall shape and stance. FDM at 6mm rewards building the profile correctly with a fine nozzle and a steady hand.

I cluster small war machines onto a single build plate and print several in one go, which makes the per-machine time essentially irrelevant. Because they are small, support scarring is proportionally more damaging, so I favour orientations that minimize overhangs on arms and legs.

Scale notes

These war machines represent units 9-15 meters tall. At 1:285 scale, a 12-meter unit should be about 42mm tall, but actual miniatures vary widely — modern sculpts are closer to 1:265 (slightly larger than true 1:285). Older metal miniatures are smaller and closer to the original ratio. Scale consistency within the range matters more than mathematical accuracy.

Base sizesHex-based (no traditional bases)

Deep Dive: 6mm war machines — from 30 to 55mm tall

This mech tactical game is 6mm (about 1:285), but a war machine's height depends on its weight class, so Light machines run 30mm tall and Assaults run 55mm. Printing proxies is about matching the publisher's modern sculpts, not a strict ratio.

Why '6mm' Is a Moving Target

The war machines represent machines 9-15 meters tall. At 1:285 scale a 12-meter machine should be about 42mm tall, but the actual range varies a lot. The publisher's modern sculpts run closer to 1:265 (slightly larger than true ratio), while older metal miniatures are smaller and closer to the original math. The scale is a family, not a single number.

Match the Range, Not the Math

The reliable approach is to pick one official miniature as your reference and match its height. I keep a single reference machine on the bench and measure every printed proxy against it. Consistency within a lance matters more than hitting a strict 1:285 ratio — the game is hex-based and scale-perfect models are the least of your worries.

FDM Limits at This Size

The machines are small but dense with detail — cockpit glass, weapon barrels, and antennas all need to read. I print the machines at 0.2mm nozzle and 0.04-0.06mm layers, and print terrain and hex tiles with a 0.4mm nozzle. Magnetizing bases makes transport easier, since small models shift around in a case.

Reference Conversions
Conversion Formula Slicer %
1:100 → 1:35 (micro scale up)50.0 ÷ 17.5285.7%
1:72 → 1:35 (small scale to model kit)50.0 ÷ 24.3205.7%

These are the validated reference steps I use when a printed model spans the small-scale ranges. They rarely apply to war machines directly — your reference miniature is the better guide.

Common Mech Tactical Mistakes
  • Scaling a Light and an Assault to the same height. Weight class differences are real and add to the game's readability.
  • Scaling to strict 1:285 math. You will undersize modern sculpts — match the range instead.
  • FDM on cockpits and antennas. At 6mm those details need a 0.2mm nozzle, or they come out as blobs.
What scale is the mech tactical game?

The mech tactical standard is 6mm epic scale focused on vehicles and war machines rather than individual infantry.

Can an FDM printer handle 6mm war machines?

Yes, the war machines are chunky enough to read well. Use a 0.2mm nozzle and print several at once on one plate.

Deep Dive: 8mm epic — Titans next to 28mm infantry

This 8mm epic-scale game is tuned so a Titan is roughly the physical size of a 28mm infantry model. That dramatic contrast is the point — and it means you should never 'fix' it by scaling up.

The 8mm Epic Scale

This game is 8mm scale (1:200), matching the older epic Titan range. Individual armoured soldiers are tiny but recognizable, and massed formations of hundreds of models fit on a single table. It is the publisher's return to epic-scale warfare, set during an epic civil war.

The Contrast Is Intentional

The scale is designed so a Titan miniature is roughly the same physical size as a 28mm infantry model. That size contrast between the tiny soldier line and the looming Titans is the whole point of the game — do not scale a Titan up "so it feels big." Also, the two epic games share the scale but not the base sizes, so keep the bases straight when you print replacements.

FDM for the Big Stuff, Skip the Infantry

At 8mm, infantry is beyond what FDM can reliably produce — the minis come out as blobs. Vehicles and Titans are larger and more forgiving, and FDM handles them fine. I print the machines at 0.2mm nozzle and 0.04mm layers. For painting at this size, contrast paints and washes beat layer-by-layer highlighting every time.

Common Epic-Scale Mistakes
  • FDM on the infantry. 8mm soldiers come out as blobs — print the vehicles and Titans instead.
  • Scaling Titans up for drama. The scale contrast is the design. Leave the numbers alone.
  • Confusing the two epic ranges' bases. Same scale, different base sizes — print to the right one for the game you play.
What scale is the epic-scale sci-fi wargame?

It is an 8mm epic scale game. The epic Titan warfare range shares its scale but uses different base sizes.

Can FDM print this epic-scale game?

Yes — Titans and vehicles are excellent FDM subjects. The tiny infantry is the limiting piece.

Deep Dive: 10mm combined arms — print the machines

This 10mm sci-fi game fields infantry barely bigger than a grain of rice and is won by tanks and dropships. The printing strategy is simple: focus on the vehicles.

The 10mm Scale

This game is 10mm scale (1:160). Individual infantry are barely larger than a grain of rice, so the game's visual impact comes from vehicle mass and formation density rather than individual detail. The publisher's range is consistent within itself, which makes cross-faction mixing straightforward.

Print the Vehicles, Skip the Infantry

FDM genuinely struggles with 10mm infantry — the bodies, weapons, and details are too fine. I skip printing the infantry and focus on the vehicles. They are the stars of this game, and they print well on FDM at 0.06mm layers with a 0.4mm nozzle.

Basing and Batch Painting

At 10mm, cohesion wins over detail. I give each faction a single base color and batch-paint the infantry in one pass, then use washes for shading. Magnetizing vehicle bases keeps the force easy to transport.

Common 10mm Mistakes
  • FDM on infantry. At 10mm it is a waste of filament — stick to official infantry.
  • Mixing 10mm with 15mm WWII models. They are close enough to feel wrong together and different enough to notice.
  • Over-detailing single models. The table reads as formations. Spend time on the vehicles, not one soldier.
What scale is the 10mm combined-arms game?

It is 10mm scale for a combined-arms sci-fi game focused on vehicles and dropships.

Can FDM handle 10mm infantry?

Vehicles print well; the small infantry is challenging. Use a fine nozzle for stand-out pieces and batch by model size.

I check whether a file means 15mm to the eyes or 1:100 total height before scaling, because the two differ. Tanks and terrain in the 15mm scale are my favourite FDM subjects — they print fast and hold detail well. Infantry at this scale is fiddly, so I reserve the fine profile for them.

Deep Dive: 15mm (1:100) — companies, not squads

This 15mm WWII game plays at 1:100, where a standard game fields dozens of tanks and hundreds of infantry on one table. Conversions here are about whole platoons, so the percentages matter more than any single model.

The 1:100 Convention

At 15mm (1:100), the miniatures are small enough to field dozens of vehicles and hundreds of infantry on a single table. The eye level works out to about 16mm on my 175cm baseline. One distinction I always check: a strict 1:100 ratio gives 17.5mm to the top of the head, while "15mm" usually means eye level — the two look similar on paper but are not identical.

The Model-Kit Jump

The validated step from 1:100 up to the 1:35 model-kit lane is 285.7%. It is a huge jump — more for display and diorama work than for tabletop play, where the 15mm size is the point.

FDM Reality at 15mm

15mm miniatures reward batch printing — you need entire platoons. I print infantry at 0.2mm nozzle and 0.06mm layers, and vehicles at 0.08mm. Magnetizing vehicle bases helps with transport. At this scale, basing has a proportionally huge visual impact, so flocking and static grass do more work than your print settings.

Common 15mm WWII Mistakes
  • Treating "15mm" and "1:100" as identical. They are close but not the same — confirm which convention your STL uses before converting.
  • FDM infantry at this scale. The rifles and webbing are too fine — keep it to vehicles and terrain.
  • Mixing in 20mm (1:72) ranges. They read noticeably larger next to 15mm. Keep a platoon in one scale.
Is the 15mm company scale 1:100?

Both terms are used. 15mm can mean eye-level while 1:100 means total height on a 175cm human, so confirm which your STL references.

Best FDM settings for 15mm WWII?

Vehicles print well at a 0.4mm nozzle and 0.1–0.2mm layers. Reserve a fine nozzle for the fiddly infantry.

Deep Dive: 28mm ranked regiments for classic fantasy

This classic range deliberately rebuilt its plastic line at the traditional 28mm fantasy scale. If you are printing an army for it, the numbers are the old-school ones — not the 32mm of the modern fantasy wargame.

The Deliberate Return to 28mm

The publisher designed this classic range at 28mm heroic scale to match the original classic fantasy battle line. That means decades of classic metal miniatures, older sculpts, and freshly printed proxies all sit together in the same ranked units without looking off.

This is smaller than the modern fantasy wargame's 32mm. Mixing the two ranges on one table produces a visible size difference — which is exactly why you need to know which lane your STL was designed in.

The 28mm Classic vs 32mm Modern Gap

When I pull a modern fantasy STL into a classic 28mm army, I convert it down to the 28mm lane. The reverse is just as common — classic fantasy STLs scaled up for a 32mm collection:

Conversion Formula Slicer %
Classic (28mm) → Modern fantasy (32mm)32 ÷ 28114.3%
Modern fantasy (32mm) → Classic (28mm)28 ÷ 3287.5%
Batch Printing Ranked Regiments

Classic fantasy armies are built from ranked blocks, so your printing strategy is volume first:

  1. Print infantry blocks at 0.4mm nozzle and 0.08mm layers. Twenty models at high detail beats five models at perfect detail.
  2. Batch by height. Rank-and-file troops are close enough in height that one build plate layout works for the whole unit.
  3. Print movement trays separately. They take a fraction of the time and glue onto printed bases cleanly.
  4. Reserve the 0.2mm nozzle for unit champions and characters. That is where your detail budget belongs.
Converting Out of the 28mm Lane

The validated steps out of 28mm cover the common side projects: 125.0% brings a classic fantasy model up to the 35mm mass-battle and superhero lane, and 178.6% scales it into the 1:35 model-kit world for display or terrain work.

Common Classic Fantasy Mistakes
  • Printing 32mm modern fantasy STLs at full size into a 28mm army. They will read as oversized next to the classic range — bring them down at 87.5%.
  • Measuring helmeted troopers to the top of the head. Eye level is the reference. Pick it with the measurement tool, not the bounding box.
  • Mixing 25mm metal and 32mm plastic in one ranked unit. Keep each unit internally consistent and the classic look holds together.
Is this scale 28mm or 32mm?

This range is 28mm measured to the eyes, matching the original classic fantasy line. It is smaller than the modern fantasy wargame's 32mm.

Can I use 32mm modern fantasy STLs in a 28mm ranked range?

Yes, but scale the 32mm file down by 87.5% to reach 28mm. Otherwise the model will look oversized in a ranked regiment.

FDM print settings

Facing accuracy is the priority, so I use a 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm layers for named characters. Rank-and-file warriors print fine at 0.4mm and 0.08mm. Always verify the eye line after scaling — it is the whole game for this range.

For named characters, proportions matter more than in any other range I print for. A 14% scale error on a face is jarring in a way it never is on an armoured soldier. I measure the eyes carefully and favour a 0.2mm nozzle so the sculpt's expression survives scaling.

One quirk I hit repeatedly: metal minis in this setting run thinner than plastic and printed alternatives. When I replace a metal hero with a printed one I add about 3% rather than scale to the raw figure height, so the new model reads the same on the table.

Deep Dive: 25mm metals and 28mm plastics in one army

This mythic fantasy setting is the one mainstream game where 25mm and 28mm miniatures fight side by side on purpose. Printing a proxy to fit means deciding which generation of the range you are matching before you touch the slicer.

The Two Scales in One Range

Older metal miniatures from the original mythic fantasy range measure closer to 25mm, while the newer plastic releases are 28mm. Both are legal in the same army, and the community has accepted the size difference as part of the range's history. Smaller races and goblin-type creatures are intentionally smaller than Men — that is proportion, not inconsistency.

That means your anchor is whatever generation dominates your collection, not a universal number.

Pick Your Anchor

If your force is mostly modern plastic, anchor at 28mm. If it is mostly classic metal, you will end up closer to 25mm in practice. The validated 28mm lane references that bracket the modern heroic side are still my sanity check:

Conversion Formula Slicer %
Mythic setting (28mm) → Modern heroic (32mm)32 ÷ 28114.3%
Modern heroic (32mm) → Mythic setting (28mm)28 ÷ 3287.5%
Realistic Proportions

This range uses realistic proportions, not heroic exaggeration — heads and hands are smaller than a modern heroic model of the same height. When I print a replacement for a named character, faces matter because they carry the character's identity. I run a 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm layers and put supports on the back and undersides so nothing touches the face.

The metal range is thinner than the plastics, so a printed replacement often looks right without adding bulk. Compare the torso width, not just the height, when you are deciding whether a proxy matches.

Vehicles and Display Pieces

Two validated steps are useful for side projects: 178.6% takes a 28mm model into the 1:35 model-kit lane for vehicles and terrain displays, and 267.9% pushes a favourite hero all the way to display scale for the cabinet.

Common Mythic Fantasy Mistakes
  • Scaling to 32mm by accident. A 114.3% up-scale is right for matching modern heroic (32mm), not for matching a collection anchored at 28mm.
  • Trusting a "25mm" label on a modern proxy. Check the eye level in the slicer against the metal miniature you are replacing.
  • Skipping facial detail on named characters. This is the one range where recognisable faces carry the game.
What scale is the mythic fantasy setting?

The mythic fantasy setting is 28mm for modern plastic kits, with older metal minis closer to 25mm. Both are played together.

How much should I scale a printed named character?

Start from a 28mm eye line, then add roughly 3% when replacing a thin metal sculpt with a printed one so it reads the same on the table.

FDM print settings

Rank-and-file infantry print at a 0.4mm nozzle and 0.1mm layers; officers and snipers get 0.06mm on a 0.2mm nozzle. Vehicles print fast and clean at 0.2mm layers. Bayonets and rifle barrels soften on FDM, so I orient those parts carefully.

I split my WWII platoon prints into two jobs. Infantry get scaled to a strict 28mm true-scale eye line. Vehicles I scale to look correct under my infantry's geometry — and that often means 1:48 rather than 1:56, because squinting soldier proportions demand a beefier hull.

The math is easy per figure, but the look is decided by the pair. I hang a test vehicle next to an infantry model before printing a motor pool. Numbers get you 90% of the way; the last 10% is eyeballing articulation and hull height, which no formula replaces.

Scale notes

This genre standard pairs 28mm true-scale infantry with 1:56 vehicles. A standard infantryman measures 28mm from foot to eye level with realistic human proportions and no heroic exaggeration. Vehicle scale is 1:56, which aligns naturally with 28mm miniatures. Many players run 1:48 model kits because modern plastic infantry have crept larger and the bulkier hulls look right alongside them.

Deep Dive: The 1:56 vehicle scale, explained

WWII platoon infantry are 28mm true scale, but the vehicles are a separate 1:56 ratio. Here is how the two pair up and what it means for your slicer.

What Scale Is the WWII Platoon Game?

WWII platoon infantry are 28mm true scale, measured to the eyes (160cm on a 175cm human baseline). This is the same convention used by older classic sci-fi sculpts, classic fantasy RPG miniatures, and most historical wargaming ranges.

The vehicle scale for this game is 1:56. This ratio means that 1 millimetre on the model equals 56 millimetres in real life. A 3-metre-tall Sherman tank should measure approximately 53.5mm on the tabletop.

Why 1:56 Works with 28mm Infantry

The 1:56 vehicle scale is paired with 28mm infantry because both use the same reference point. A 175cm human in 1:56 scale is approximately 31.25mm tall to the top of the head, which puts the eye level at about 28mm. The math lines up.

Common WWII Platoon Printing Mistakes
  • Printing vehicles at 100% when they are designed for 1:35. A 1:35 tank printed at full size will be nearly twice as long as it should be next to your 28mm infantry. Always check the STL description for the intended scale.
  • Scaling infantry by total height instead of eye level. A model with a raised arm or tall helmet will have a misleading bounding box. Measure from the foot contact point to the eyes, use that as your reference dimension.
  • Using 100% infill on vehicles. Most WWII platoon vehicles are hollow in the real kit. For 3D prints, use 15-20% grid infill. It saves filament and the model will still be durable enough for regular handling.
Is the WWII platoon scale 28mm or 1:56?

Both. Infantry are 28mm true scale to the eyes, and the official vehicle scale is 1:56. Many players prefer 1:48 model kits because they look correct next to bulkier modern plastic infantry.

How do I bring a 1:35 vehicle STL down for a WWII platoon game?

Scale a 1:35 vehicle to 62.5% to reach 1:56. If you target 1:48 instead, use a smaller reduction so the hull lands in the 1:48 sweet spot.

Printing RPG Miniatures in Bulk
  • Print multiple miniatures at once by arranging them on the build plate with at least 5mm of spacing between each model.
  • Use the same layer height for all models in the batch. Switching between 0.06mm and 0.1mm per model wastes time on filament changes and recalibration.
  • Print bases separately. Flat circular bases print in minutes and you can glue the miniatures on after removing supports.
Common RPG Scaling Mistakes
  • Printing a dragon at 100% when it was designed for 28mm scale. A dragon STL labelled "for 28mm" is already the correct size for a Medium-scale game. If you want an Ancient dragon that towers over the party, scale it to 200-400%.
  • Using a 0.4mm nozzle for tiny creatures. A goblin's face at 0.2mm layer height with a 0.4mm nozzle will lack definition. Swap to a 0.2mm nozzle for anything Small or smaller.
  • Scaling by bounding box. A dragon with outstretched wings will have a huge bounding box that does not reflect its body size. Measure from foot to eye, ignore the wing span.
What scale are classic fantasy RPG miniatures?

A Medium humanoid like a human is 28mm true scale to the eyes. Smaller and larger creatures map to the RPG size categories rather than a single number.

What does 28mm mean for a classic fantasy RPG?

28mm represents a Medium creature such as a human, elf, or orc. Save this as your reference before scaling larger or smaller monsters.

The Scale Quirk

These models are nominally 28mm but measure closer to 29-30mm in practice thanks to scale creep across the range. Match the Metal, Not the Label

The reliable way is the caliper. Most third-party proxies are sculpted slim and land close to the range as-is; if anything, I scale up a touch rather than down. The validated 114.3% step (28mm → 32mm) overshoots the range's real-world 29-30mm, so treat this as its own lane and verify with a measurement.

The 'Any Miniature' Rule

The official miniatures for the fantasy game are 28mm true scale, but the game is explicitly miniature-agnostic — any 28mm or 32mm miniatures work. The sci-fi version leans toward 28mm sci-fi but accepts the same range. That flexibility makes both games a natural fit for a 3D printed collection.

Pick an Anchor and Stay Consistent

The only real rule is internal consistency. Pick 28mm or 32mm for a warband and hold it across every model in the group. The validated step between the lanes is:

Conversion Formula Slicer %
Fantasy skirmish (28mm) → Modern heroic (32mm)32 ÷ 28114.3%
Modern heroic (32mm) → Fantasy skirmish (28mm)28 ÷ 3287.5%
What to Print

This is one of the best games for 3D printing experimentation. I print warbands in batches at 0.4mm nozzle and 0.08mm layers for playability, and save the 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm for wizards and named characters. Terrain is half the game — frozen ruins for the fantasy version, sci-fi corridors for the sci-fi one — and it prints great on FDM at 0.1mm layers.

Mixing Ranges

If you want to pull in a 35mm miniature as a guest star, the validated step up from the 28mm lane is 125.0%. That lands the model in the 35mm lane alongside them rather than trying to squeeze a bigger sculpt down to your warband's scale.

Common Miniature-Agnostic Mistakes
  • Mixing 25mm metals with 32mm STLs in one warband. Each warband should look like it came from the same place — pick one lane and stick to it.
  • Spending hours on a rank-and-file thug. Playability models read fine at 0.08mm layers. Reserve the fine detail for wizards and captains.
  • Skipping terrain. These are terrain games. The board sells the theme more than any single model.
What scale are the miniature-agnostic skirmish games?

Both are 28mm true scale and are designed to be built from mixed miniature ranges.

Why do my modular warband pieces look uneven?

Different sculptors drift from 28mm. Scale every printed piece to a strict 28mm eye line so the mixed warband coheres.

The 28mm Baseline

Batch Printing for Regiments

This steampunk fantasy wargame launched as 28mm and the publisher now calls the range 30mm. Printing proxies means accepting that '30mm' is not a conversion target — it is a bracket between 28mm and 32mm.

28mm, 30mm, or Both?

The game was originally marketed as 28mm and reclassified to 30mm later in its life. The miniatures use chunky heroic proportions — exaggerated weapons and armor, beefy silhouettes. Both labels are accepted in the community, and the range's own models span the bracket depending on when they were sculpted.

Where Printed Proxies Land

Most STL files are labeled either "28mm heroic" or "32mm heroic." The game's 30mm sits between the two. In practice I treat it as 28mm heroic when I print proxies, then verify with the caliper against a reference war machine or infantry model. If a file runs big or small, I adjust by a touch and re-measure — the label is a starting point, not the answer.

The Bracket in Numbers

There is no validated "30mm" conversion in the matrix, so the two validated references that bracket the lane are the ones I use:

Conversion Formula Slicer %

Scaling a proxy all the way to strict 32mm usually overshoots a real army — that step is the top of the bracket, not the middle.

FDM Settings for War Machines

The bulky mechanical designs are forgiving on FDM — flat armor panels hide layer lines, and the war machines are big enough that I run a 0.4mm nozzle at 0.1mm layers for the machines. Heavy infantry and characters get a 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm. The metal originals are heavy, so printed alternatives are noticeably lighter and easier to transport.

Common Steampunk Wargame Mistakes
  • Forcing a 30mm army to strict 32mm scale. Your proxies will read oversized next to the range — stay in the 28mm heroic lane.
  • Measuring to the top of a war machine's cab. Eye level is the reference even on machines; the cab is usually a raised detail, not the scale point.
  • FDM on heavy-troop trim. The heavy troops have a lot of small trim that FDM softens first.

It is 30mm scale, stockier than 28mm with exaggerated armor and weapons.

Should I scale a 30mm proxy up to 32mm?

You can, but the range is designed at 30mm. Keeping everything at 30mm gives a more coherent force than guessing.

Deep Dive: Heroic 32mm vs True-Scale 28mm

The modern sci-fi epic standard has one of the most confusing scale landscapes in tabletop gaming. Between modern heroic (32mm) soldiers, classic true-scale (28mm) sculpts, older casts, and third-party proxies, knowing what percentage to type into your slicer is not always obvious.

The Two Scale Generations

The publisher uses two distinct scales depending on the range:

  • Modern heroic (32mm) / newer sculpts: 32mm heroic scale, measured to the eyes (160cm on a 175cm baseline)
  • Classic true-scale (28mm) / older sculpts: 28mm true scale, also measured to the eyes

A modern heroic soldier is roughly 14% taller than a classic true-scale soldier. This is not scale creep — it is intentional. The newer range was designed with truer human proportions, which means longer legs and a taller frame.

Conversion Cheat Sheet
Conversion Formula Slicer %
Classic (28mm) → Modern heroic (32mm)32 ÷ 28114.3%
Modern heroic (32mm) → Classic (28mm)28 ÷ 3287.5%
28mm → 40mm (large armoured elite / heavy infantry)40 ÷ 28142.9%
32mm → 40mm40 ÷ 32125.0%
28mm → 75mm (display scale)75 ÷ 28267.9%
How to Scale a Modern Heroic Proxy on FDM

Most 32mm sci-fi epic STL files you find online are designed for 32mm heroic scale. Here is how to handle them on an FDM printer:

  1. Check the sculptor's baseline. If the description says "32mm scale" or "heroic 32mm," you can print it as-is for a modern heroic army.
  2. Measure eye level in your slicer. Import the STL, use the measurement tool, and check the distance from the bottom of the foot to the eyes. If it is not 32mm (or close), scale it.
  3. Set your layer height to 0.08mm. This is the sweet spot for 32mm heroic miniatures on FDM. Detail is good enough for tabletop distance, and print time stays reasonable.
  4. Use a 0.2mm nozzle for faces. If you have one, swap to a 0.2mm nozzle for character models. The difference in facial detail is significant.
What About Vehicles?

32mm sci-fi epic vehicles use a different scaling convention. An armoured transport chassis is designed to look correct next to 32mm modern heroic models. If you are printing a vehicle STL labelled "for 28mm," scale it up to 114.3% to match your modern heroic force.

For larger vehicles like super-heavy tanks or Titans, scale by comparison to a known reference model rather than using a formula. Vehicle proportions vary too much between sculptors for a universal percentage.

Is the sci-fi epic standard 28mm or 32mm scale?

The modern sci-fi epic standard is 32mm heroic scale measured to the eyes. Older classic true-scale (28mm) and classic sculpts are closer to 28mm true scale. Scale up 28mm STLs to 114.3% to match a modern heroic (32mm) army.

How do I scale a sci-fi proxy STL?

Measure the file's eye level in your slicer first. If it is a 28mm classic true-scale (28mm) proxy aiming to stand next to modern heroic (32mm), apply a uniform 114.3% scale. If the file is already 32mm, print it as-is.

What is the best FDM profile for 32mm sci-fi infantry?

A 0.4mm nozzle at 0.08mm layers handles rank-and-file well. Swap to a 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm layers for character models so faces and weapons stay crisp.

FDM print settings

Character models get a 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm layers for clean edges on armor and chainmail. Centerpiece dragons, daemons, and undead warlords benefit from the same profile on the faces. FDM handles terrain and large monsters well at 0.1mm layers.

I treat modern fantasy conversions in two buckets. Files designed for the current 32mm range print as-is, while classic-generation fantasy sculpts and the many '28mm fantasy' STLs get scaled up to 114.3% to match. It is the same number as the sci-fi epic standard because both ranges share the heroic 175cm baseline.

Modern fantasy models have dramatic poses — flowing cloaks, extended banners, weapon arms swung wide. I always check the slicer's bounding box after scaling because a 14% upscale on a wide pose can push a model past the build plate on small beds. I plan orientation before I commit to supports.

Deep Dive: Classic fantasy, new plastic — the 28mm to 32mm jump

The modern fantasy wargame sits at 32mm heroic, but most fantasy collections are full of older 28mm models. Knowing which side of that line your STLs sit on is the whole game when you are printing a mixed collection.

Where the Modern 32mm Sits in Scale

Every modern fantasy release is 32mm heroic scale, measured to the eyes — the same convention as the modern heroic (32mm) sci-fi standard. Older classic fantasy battle miniatures are 28mm heroic. Both ranges still share tables in the modern fantasy game, and the size gap is part of the range's history.

Conversion Formula Slicer %
Classic fantasy (28mm) → Modern fantasy (32mm)32 ÷ 28114.3%
Modern fantasy (32mm) → Classic fantasy (28mm)28 ÷ 3287.5%
Mixing Classic Fantasy and New Plastic

If your force is mostly new plastic, treat 32mm as your anchor and scale any older 28mm fantasy STLs up at 114.3%. If you are printing a classic regimental army to sit next to older-era sculpts, you usually want to keep it at 32mm to hold the line — an undersized rank reads instantly across the table.

The reverse matters too. A modern fantasy STL dropped into a classic 28mm collection will tower over the old metal heroes; bring it down at 87.5% if you want it to blend in.

FDM Settings for the Modern Fantasy Game
Model Type Nozzle Layer Height Notes
Characters and heroes0.2mm0.06mmSharpest edges on armor and faces
Rank-and-file infantry0.4mm0.08mmGood balance of speed and detail
Monsters and centerpieces0.4mm0.1mmBig surfaces hide layer lines well
Terrain0.4mm0.2mmUse grid infill for strength
Scaling Centrepiece Models

Big centerpiece monsters are where this scale really shows. If a dragon or daemon STL is designed for a smaller lane and you want it to dominate the board, the validated steps up from the 32mm lane are what I reach for: 234.4% takes a 32mm hero into full display territory, and 109.4% steps it up to the 35mm mass-battle and superhero lane for a slightly larger presence next to those scales.

Common Modern Fantasy Scaling Mistakes
  • Printing 28mm fantasy STLs at full size in a 32mm army. If the sculptor says "28mm," you need the 114.3% step to sit level with modern plastic.
  • Running a 0.4mm nozzle on character faces. The heroes carry most of their personality in the face and helmet trim — swap to a 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm layers.
  • Measuring to the top of a helmet. Scale is set by eye level. A tall helmet or hair tuft will give you a misleading bounding box — measure foot to eyes in the slicer.
What scale is the modern fantasy wargame?

The modern fantasy wargame uses 32mm heroic scale for new releases, the same baseline as the 32mm sci-fi epic standard. Modern sculpts are designed to this size.

How do I convert old classic fantasy STLs to the modern 32mm range?

Scale classic-generation 28mm fantasy sculpts up by 114.3% to match the modern 32mm range. The two otherwise show a noticeable height gap.

Deep Dive: The 32mm rule-agnostic playground

This miniature-agnostic sci-fi wargame has no official range — it is built for printed and proxy collections. That means you set the scale, and the only rule that matters is keeping one scale across your whole force.

No Official Range, No Wrong Answer

This game is miniature-agnostic by design — it works with whatever you own. The 32mm recommendation aligns with the modern heroic standards and the majority of 3D printed STL files, but a 28mm classic collection works just as well. What the rules actually care about is base sizes, not model heights.

Pick a Standard for Your Army
Conversion Formula Slicer %
Classic (28mm) → Agnostic standard (32mm)32 ÷ 28114.3%
Agnostic standard (32mm) → Classic (28mm)28 ÷ 3287.5%

Commit to one lane for the whole army. The only real scale mistake in this game is switching mid-force.

Base Sizes Drive the Rules

The game's unit categories are keyed to base sizes — infantry, heavy infantry, cavalry, and so on. The game is forgiving about visual consistency precisely because the bases do the rules work. Print your models to fit the correct base category and the army plays correctly even if the sculpts vary.

FDM Settings

Since there are no official models to match, print whatever you want. I use a 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm layers for characters and a 0.4mm nozzle at 0.1mm for rank-and-file. PLA with high fan from the first few layers gives clean overhangs on capes and weapon barrels.

Common Agnostic Scale Mistakes
  • Mixing 28mm and 32mm mid-army. The rules do not care, but the table will look inconsistent. Pick one lane.
  • Ignoring the base size chart. It drives the rules — a proxy on the wrong base category changes how it plays.
  • Over-investing in rank-and-file detail. Across-the-table models read fine at 0.1mm. Spend detail on heroes and monsters.
What scale is the miniature-agnostic sci-fi wargame?

It uses a 32mm heroic baseline, matching the modern sci-fi epic standard.

Why do my community proxies not match?

Different sculptors drift from 32mm. Measure each STL's eye line on import and scale it back to 32mm.

The Forgiving Weathered Look

The post-apocalyptic theme is a gift for FDM printers. Rust, grime, scratches, and radiation damage are thematically correct — they hide layer lines naturally. I lean into weathering on everything and it looks intentional rather than like a print artifact.

FDM Settings

Common Post-Apocalyptic Mistakes
  • Printing "28mm scale" STLs at full size next to official 32mm models. Use the 114.3% step to sit level with the range.

  • Skipping terrain. Ruined buildings and vehicles are a big part of the game and the best FDM print targets in the whole range.

  • Mixing 28mm classic models with 32mm warband fighters. In a small skirmish game the size gap reads fast. Keep the warband in one lane.
  • Scaling by bounding box. Dynamic poses with sweeping weapons inflate the box. Measure foot to eye.
  • Over-engineering rank-and-file prints. The best quality-per-model ratio is on leaders and champions, not the chaff.
What scale is the fantasy skirmish game?

It uses the same 32mm heroic scale as the modern fantasy wargame, played as a small warband skirmish game.

Do fantasy skirmish STLs match the 32mm modern fantasy range?

They share the same basis, but sculptors drift. Measure each STL's eye line and scale to a 32mm baseline for cohesion.

Deep Dive: 35mm eye level — why armoured troopers tower over heroic soldiers

The sci-fi mass-battle game is 35mm to the eyes (35.7mm on my 175cm baseline), which puts it bigger than the 32mm heroic standard and smaller than the 40mm sci-fi skirmish scale. Getting proxies to match means working from that eye-level number, not the top of the helmet.

What 35mm Actually Means

The 35mm designation is an eye-level measurement. An armoured trooper's eyes sit 35.7mm above the base, and the full miniature reaches about 40mm to the top of the helmet. That works out to roughly 1:47 scale on a 1678mm eye-height reference — and it is why common 1:48 sci-fi model kits sit so close to the range.

The takeaway: measure to the eyes in your slicer. If you measure to the top of the helmet you will undersize every proxy.

35mm vs Classic 28mm

The jump from classic 28mm systems into the 35mm lane is bigger than it looks on paper: 125.0% up from 28mm, or 80.0% down if you are scaling 35mm STLs for a 28mm game. Either way, the models end up clearly different in bulk, not just height.

FDM and Smooth Armor

Armoured trooper plate is made of smooth, unbroken panels — exactly the surface where FDM layer lines show. I print infantry at 0.06mm layers or finer, and walker-style vehicles at 0.1mm. When I scale a proxy, I enable the chain-link lock in my slicer so the ratio stays uniform across all three axes.

Common Mass-Battle Scale Mistakes

  • Trusting a "32mm" label on a proxy. Verify the eye-level height in the slicer before committing to a long print.
What scale is the sci-fi mass-battle game?

It is 35mm eye-level scale (1:47). An armoured trooper measures about 35.7mm to the eyes and about 40mm to the top of the helmet.

Upscale a 32mm file by 109.4% to reach the 35mm eye level. Keep uniform scaling locked.

True Scale vs Heroic Scale

Deep Dive: 1:27 ships, no infantry to confuse the math

The 1:27 Convention

This game is 1:27 ratio scale, used across every ship in the game — no infantry at all. For a human-sized reference that works out to roughly 59.3mm eye level and 64.8mm to the top of the head. Ships range from a small fighter you can hold in your palm to a spacecraft that fills most of the table, so the math stays clean but the print sizes swing wildly.

Printing the Ships

1:27 ships are large enough for FDM to handle detail well. I use a 0.2mm nozzle at 0.08mm layers for cockpit glass, panel lines, and engine details, and a 0.4mm nozzle at 0.12mm layers for large ships when speed matters. The hulls are smooth and show layer lines easily, so print at the finest layer height you have patience for, and orient engines and cockpits upward to keep supports on hidden undersides.

Matching the Pre-Painted Plastic

The Die-Cast Convention

Adding Infantry and Printed Gear

Common Vehicular Combat Mistakes

How these FDM profiles are tested

By kitsorix, 3D printing hobbyist

Every profile here starts from a 175cm human baseline with eye-level at 160cm, then gets a real test print. FDM materials are dimensionally stable within 0.5%, so the scale you dial in is the scale you get.

I print on a Bambu Lab A1 Mini with PLA. These nozzle and layer-height recommendations are what actually works for me on that machine — they are a solid starting point, not a guarantee. Your printer, filament, and environment will introduce their own variables.

If a profile reads differently on your machine, send it to me and I will add a note.

FDM printing FAQ

Is the sci-fi epic standard 28mm or 32mm scale?
The modern sci-fi epic standard is 32mm heroic scale measured to the eyes. Older classic true-scale (28mm) and classic sculpts are closer to 28mm true scale. Scale up 28mm STLs to 114.3% to match a modern heroic (32mm) army.
How do I scale a sci-fi proxy STL?
Measure the file's eye level in your slicer first. If it is a 28mm classic true-scale (28mm) proxy aiming to stand next to modern heroic (32mm), apply a uniform 114.3% scale. If the file is already 32mm, print it as-is.
What is the best FDM profile for 32mm sci-fi infantry?
A 0.4mm nozzle at 0.08mm layers handles rank-and-file well. Swap to a 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm layers for character models so faces and weapons stay crisp.
What scale is the modern fantasy wargame?
The modern fantasy wargame uses 32mm heroic scale for new releases, the same baseline as the 32mm sci-fi epic standard. Modern sculpts are designed to this size.
How do I convert old classic fantasy STLs to the modern 32mm range?
Scale classic-generation 28mm fantasy sculpts up by 114.3% to match the modern 32mm range. The two otherwise show a noticeable height gap.
Is this scale 28mm or 32mm?
This range is 28mm measured to the eyes, matching the original classic fantasy line. It is smaller than the modern fantasy wargame's 32mm.
Can I use 32mm modern fantasy STLs in a 28mm ranked range?
Yes, but scale the 32mm file down by 87.5% to reach 28mm. Otherwise the model will look oversized in a ranked regiment.
What scale is the mythic fantasy setting?
The mythic fantasy setting is 28mm for modern plastic kits, with older metal minis closer to 25mm. Both are played together.
How much should I scale a printed named character?
Start from a 28mm eye line, then add roughly 3% when replacing a thin metal sculpt with a printed one so it reads the same on the table.
Is the WWII platoon scale 28mm or 1:56?
Both. Infantry are 28mm true scale to the eyes, and the official vehicle scale is 1:56. Many players prefer 1:48 model kits because they look correct next to bulkier modern plastic infantry.
How do I bring a 1:35 vehicle STL down for a WWII platoon game?
Scale a 1:35 vehicle to 62.5% to reach 1:56. If you target 1:48 instead, use a smaller reduction so the hull lands in the 1:48 sweet spot.
What scale are classic fantasy RPG miniatures?
A Medium humanoid like a human is 28mm true scale to the eyes. Smaller and larger creatures map to the RPG size categories rather than a single number.
What does 28mm mean for a classic fantasy RPG?
28mm represents a Medium creature such as a human, elf, or orc. Save this as your reference before scaling larger or smaller monsters.
What scale is the sci-fi mass-battle game?
It is 35mm eye-level scale (1:47). An armoured trooper measures about 35.7mm to the eyes and about 40mm to the top of the helmet.
How do I scale a 32mm STL up to the 35mm lane?
Upscale a 32mm file by 109.4% to reach the 35mm eye level. Keep uniform scaling locked.
What scale is the sci-fi skirmish game?
It is 40mm scale, the largest standard space-opera game scale, with the villain reaching about 43mm total height.
How does 40mm compare with the 35mm mass-battle scale?
The 40mm scale is larger. A 35mm mass-battle STL scales up by 114.3% to match the 40mm baseline.
What scale is the superhero skirmish game?
It is 35mm scale, though proportions are exaggerated heroic style for readability and painting.
How do I scale a proxy for the 35mm superhero lane?
Set your STL to a 35mm baseline and lock uniform XYZ scaling. Keep poses centered so scaled models stay on the build plate.
What scale is the gothic pulp skirmish game?
It is 32mm heroic scale. Its models are known for slim, stylized silhouettes and ornate bases.
Why do my gothic pulp prints break?
Thin staffs and extended weapon arms are fragile on FDM. Print upright with adequate support contact and a fine layer profile.
What scale is the anime sci-fi skirmish range?
It is 28mm true scale with realistic human proportions rather than heroic exaggeration.
Best FDM settings for this sci-fi range?
Use a fine 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm layers to protect the delicate gear detail the range is known for.
What scale is the steampunk fantasy wargame?
It is 30mm scale, stockier than 28mm with exaggerated armor and weapons.
Should I scale a 30mm proxy up to 32mm?
You can, but the range is designed at 30mm. Keeping everything at 30mm gives a more coherent force than guessing.
What scale are the miniature-agnostic skirmish games?
Both are 28mm true scale and are designed to be built from mixed miniature ranges.
Why do my modular warband pieces look uneven?
Different sculptors drift from 28mm. Scale every printed piece to a strict 28mm eye line so the mixed warband coheres.
What scale is the ranked fantasy mass-battle game?
It is a 28mm mass-battle fantasy game where entire regiments share a footprint.
How do I keep a regiment consistent when printing?
Save one 28mm slicer profile, apply it to every copy of the STL, and print the whole batch with identical settings.
What scale is the mech tactical game?
The mech tactical standard is 6mm epic scale focused on vehicles and war machines rather than individual infantry.
Can an FDM printer handle 6mm war machines?
Yes, the war machines are chunky enough to read well. Use a 0.2mm nozzle and print several at once on one plate.
Is the 15mm company scale 1:100?
Both terms are used. 15mm can mean eye-level while 1:100 means total height on a 175cm human, so confirm which your STL references.
Best FDM settings for 15mm WWII?
Vehicles print well at a 0.4mm nozzle and 0.1–0.2mm layers. Reserve a fine nozzle for the fiddly infantry.
What scale is the 10mm combined-arms game?
It is 10mm scale for a combined-arms sci-fi game focused on vehicles and dropships.
Can FDM handle 10mm infantry?
Vehicles print well; the small infantry is challenging. Use a fine nozzle for stand-out pieces and batch by model size.
What scale is the epic-scale sci-fi wargame?
It is an 8mm epic scale game. The epic Titan warfare range shares its scale but uses different base sizes.
Can FDM print this epic-scale game?
Yes — Titans and vehicles are excellent FDM subjects. The tiny infantry is the limiting piece.
What scale is the miniature-agnostic sci-fi wargame?
It uses a 32mm heroic baseline, matching the modern sci-fi epic standard.
Why do my community proxies not match?
Different sculptors drift from 32mm. Measure each STL's eye line on import and scale it back to 32mm.
What scale is the post-apocalyptic wargame?
It is 32mm scale, matching common modern miniature ranges.
Does the wasteland theme hide print artifacts?
Often yes — the worn, rough aesthetic suits FDM layer lines on terrain and props better than clean sci-fi armor.
What scale does the vehicular combat game use?
It uses toy cars around 1:64 scale, but the actual size depends on the die-cast cars you bring.
How do I scale vehicular combat parts?
Scale weapon and crew STLs against your physical toy car, since die-cast sizes vary between manufacturers.
What scale is the sci-fi skirmish game?
It uses the same 32mm heroic scale as the sci-fi epic standard, played with small squads.
Should each operative scale the same?
Yes — keep every operative at a 32mm baseline so the squad reads as one coherent unit.
What scale is the gang warfare skirmish game?
It is a 32mm skirmish game centered on gangs and dense hive-terrain battles.
Is this gang game good for 3D printing?
Extremely — both the gangs and the modular hive terrain print well, and layer lines suit the worn industrial aesthetic.
What scale is the fantasy skirmish game?
It uses the same 32mm heroic scale as the modern fantasy wargame, played as a small warband skirmish game.
Do fantasy skirmish STLs match the 32mm modern fantasy range?
They share the same basis, but sculptors drift. Measure each STL's eye line and scale to a 32mm baseline for cohesion.
What scale is the dogfight game?
It is a 1:27 ship-scale game. All models are vehicles and fighters rather than infantry.
How do I print a 1:27 ship without support marks?
Orient the hull to keep cockpit and wings clear of supports, use a fine nozzle for detail, and check large ships fit your bed.
What scale is this fantasy mass-battle game?
It is a 35mm fantasy mass-battle game, larger than the 28–32mm mainstream ranges.
Does 35mm fantasy match the 35mm sci-fi mass-battle scale?
Both are around 35mm, but never assume interchangeability — scale each proxy from a clean 35mm baseline by eye line.
